performers: Philharmonic Symphony Orchestra of London; Artur Rodzinski, conductor
question: How different can the same dance material sound when its weight moves between low strings, solo violin and low woodwinds?
intro: A compact scherzo puts heavy-footed low strings beside a much lighter solo-violin trio. Its returns are not photocopies: instrumentation changes the character of material you already know.

sections.label: Scherzo
sections.mNote: Low strings begin the three-beat dance.

sections.label: Trio · approximate
sections.mNote: Solo violin and harp lighten the dance.

sections.label: Altered return · approximate
sections.mNote: Low woodwinds and pizzicato recolour returning material.

sections.label: Compressed close
sections.mNote: Shortened final gestures recover orchestral weight.

cues.title: The dance starts low
cues.text: Cellos and double basses begin the scherzo without the rest of the orchestra. Count three beats, then notice how accents and the melody’s shape make that simple metre feel less smooth than a conventional ballroom waltz.
cues.evidence: https://imslp.tw/uploads/PMLASIA01319-Shostakovich_Fifth_Symphony%2C__Op__47_-_Full_Score.pdf, printed p. 52, rehearsal 48: Allegretto, 3/4, cellos and basses alone. cache/analysis/shostakovich-5-allegretto.txt; source: https://archive.org/details/lp_symphony-no-5-opus-47_dmitri-shostakovich-philharmonic-symphony: opening low-level window rises markedly by 0:05. The metre comes from the score, not beat-estimation software.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: One side, two movements
cues.text: On Westminster WN 18001, this scherzo shares side one with the Moderato. The source supplies it as a separate track; that digital division does not imply a separate recording session.
cues.evidence: Original label, PDF p. 3, side 1, matrix XTV 22720: https://archive.org/download/lp_symphony-no-5-opus-47_dmitri-shostakovich-philharmonic-symphony/lp_symphony-no-5-opus-47_dmitri-shostakovich-philharmonic-symphony.pdf . Track order also appears in https://archive.org/download/lp_symphony-no-5-opus-47_dmitri-shostakovich-philharmonic-symphony/disc-metadata.json . No musical event is asserted at this context timestamp.

cues.title: A heavier dancing body
cues.text: The opening span has gained wind and brass weight. Listen to the contrast between a strongly projected tune and the short accompanying steps: adding instruments does not remove the dance’s deliberately uneven profile.
cues.evidence: https://imslp.tw/uploads/PMLASIA01319-Shostakovich_Fifth_Symphony%2C__Op__47_-_Full_Score.pdf, printed pp. 54–62, especially rehearsal 56: horn-led writing with bassoons, low strings and percussion. cache/analysis/shostakovich-5-allegretto.txt; source: https://archive.org/details/lp_symphony-no-5-opus-47_dmitri-shostakovich-philharmonic-symphony: relatively forceful windows near 0:55–1:00 and 1:15–1:20 precede the withdrawal at 1:28. This is a regional, not bar-level, horn attribution.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A violin changes the scale
cues.text: The trio gives a solo violin a far lighter setting, with harp and plucked strings. The dance does not need to stop for the character to change: fewer players, a higher register and shorter accompaniment transform its manner.
cues.evidence: https://imslp.tw/uploads/PMLASIA01319-Shostakovich_Fifth_Symphony%2C__Op__47_-_Full_Score.pdf, printed pp. 64–65, rehearsals 57–59: solo violin, harp and pizzicato cellos, followed by flute. cache/analysis/shostakovich-5-allegretto.txt; source: https://archive.org/details/lp_symphony-no-5-opus-47_dmitri-shostakovich-philharmonic-symphony: strongest boundary at 1:28; levels remain about −26 to −28 dB through 1:30–2:00. The cue covers the solo-led trio, not an exact handoff to flute.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Rodzinski had an earlier connection
cues.text: Rodzinski conducted the first American performance of the Fifth in an NBC Symphony broadcast on 9 April 1938. His Westminster account therefore came after a long association with the work; it is not that 1938 broadcast.
cues.evidence: Harlow Robinson, Boston Symphony Orchestra work note, performance-history paragraph: https://www.bso.org/works/symphony-no-5-shostakovich . The source used here is the Westminster LP, not the NBC performance or Rodzinski’s 1942 recording.

cues.title: The return changes clothes
cues.text: The scherzo’s return is not a simple replay of the opening orchestration. Low bassoons and contrabassoon recover the material, while plucked strings help give the returning dance a different surface.
cues.evidence: https://imslp.tw/uploads/PMLASIA01319-Shostakovich_Fifth_Symphony%2C__Op__47_-_Full_Score.pdf, printed pp. 71–72, rehearsals 65–67: bassoons/contrabassoon followed by pizzicato string entries. cache/analysis/shostakovich-5-allegretto.txt; source: https://archive.org/details/lp_symphony-no-5-opus-47_dmitri-shostakovich-philharmonic-symphony: the quieter 2:45–3:05 region lies between stronger trio and returning-tutti activity. The 2:45 section boundary is approximate.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The label names London
cues.text: The original label credits the Philharmonic Symphony Orchestra of London. Later reissue documentation calls the orchestra the Royal Philharmonic and dates the sessions to October 1954. The dossier keeps that identification separate from what the original LP itself proves.
cues.evidence: LP label: https://archive.org/download/lp_symphony-no-5-opus-47_dmitri-shostakovich-philharmonic-symphony/lp_symphony-no-5-opus-47_dmitri-shostakovich-philharmonic-symphony.pdf , pp. 3–4. Reissue MVCW-18008: https://ci.nii.ac.jp/ncid/BA40424469 . Linking the reissue session details to this LP is recorded as inferred, not original-label documentation.

cues.title: A compact final flourish
cues.text: The close packs a strong final burst into a short space, then releases it quickly. Compare its brevity with the long preparations of the first movement: here a small gesture can close the whole argument.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/shostakovich-5-allegretto.txt; source: https://archive.org/details/lp_symphony-no-5-opus-47_dmitri-shostakovich-philharmonic-symphony: late boundaries at 3:54, 4:10 and 4:14; level reaches −9.1 dB at 4:00, retreats to −22.5 at 4:15 and ends at 267.8 seconds. Final orchestral gestures are visible at https://imslp.tw/uploads/PMLASIA01319-Shostakovich_Fifth_Symphony%2C__Op__47_-_Full_Score.pdf, printed p. 84, rehearsal 74.

transitions.title: The orchestra makes room for one violin
transitions.how: The strongly projected scherzo yields to solo violin, harp and plucked strings. A reduction in weight and a new foreground player make the join audible without changing the basic three-beat dance frame. The marker is the measured regional withdrawal, not a bar-perfect solo entrance.
transitions.evidence: https://imslp.tw/uploads/PMLASIA01319-Shostakovich_Fifth_Symphony%2C__Op__47_-_Full_Score.pdf, pp. 64–65, rehearsal 57. cache/analysis/shostakovich-5-allegretto.txt; source: https://archive.org/details/lp_symphony-no-5-opus-47_dmitri-shostakovich-philharmonic-symphony: strongest boundary at 1:28; level falls from −10.0 at 1:20 to −26.5 at 1:30.

transitions.title: Familiar material returns in low woodwinds
transitions.how: The returning scherzo material changes its instrumental footing. Bassoons and contrabassoon take a role first occupied by cellos and basses; pizzicato strings then alter its articulation further. This is a varied return, not a copied opening.
transitions.evidence: https://imslp.tw/uploads/PMLASIA01319-Shostakovich_Fifth_Symphony%2C__Op__47_-_Full_Score.pdf, pp. 71–72, rehearsals 65–67, compared with p. 52. cache/analysis/shostakovich-5-allegretto.txt; source: https://archive.org/details/lp_symphony-no-5-opus-47_dmitri-shostakovich-philharmonic-symphony: quieter level region at 2:45–3:05 and renewed activity after 3:04. Exact return bar has not been aligned.

transitions.title: A last gathering of weight
transitions.how: The closing gestures recover the larger ensemble and compress the remaining business. The recorded level rises again before the short final withdrawal; no prolonged transition or new contrasting middle section intervenes.
transitions.evidence: cache/analysis/shostakovich-5-allegretto.txt; source: https://archive.org/details/lp_symphony-no-5-opus-47_dmitri-shostakovich-philharmonic-symphony: boundaries at 3:50/3:54; −17.4 dB at 3:50 rises to −9.1 at 4:00. Closing score context: https://imslp.tw/uploads/PMLASIA01319-Shostakovich_Fifth_Symphony%2C__Op__47_-_Full_Score.pdf, p. 84.

source.title: Symphony No. 5 — Muzgiz M. 16313 Г, historical full score
source.locator: Printed pp. 52–84; PDF pp. 54–86. Viewed score is public domain in Taiwan, not cleared for EU/US republication; exact performing edition unknown. Selected passage snapshots with approximate timing from cache/analysis/shostakovich-5-allegretto.txt; source: https://archive.org/details/lp_symphony-no-5-opus-47_dmitri-shostakovich-philharmonic-symphony, not a complete instrument-on/off transcription.

timeline.note: Horn-led later opening span, p. 62/rehearsal 56; regional placement before the 1:28 withdrawal.
Solo violin with harp and pizzicato cellos, pp. 64–65; violin solo is a section player, represented within violins-1.
Recoloured return, pp. 71–72/rehearsals 65–66; snapshot includes successive low-wind and pizzicato-string entries, not one simultaneous attack.
Final orchestral gestures, p. 84/rehearsal 74, including xylophone within percussion; a passage-level closing snapshot.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Philharmonic Symphony Orchestra of London (orchestra), Artur Rodzinski (conductor)
fields.note: Original sleeve and labels establish the displayed credit. Later Westminster reissue documentation and the publisher’s discography identify the orchestra as the Royal Philharmonic Orchestra. That cross-identification is not substituted silently for the original label credit; individual players and soloists are not established.

fields.label: Work version
fields.note: The work and movement are identified, but the exact performing edition is not. The historical score supports broad orchestration and formal observations, not a claim of bar-exact agreement with Rodzinski’s materials. The movement is the entire supplied source track; no local audio edit is made. The set’s finale has a separately disclosed reported cut.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: CiNii’s record for Westminster MVCW-18008 explicitly gives this range; the publisher independently lists the Rodzinski/Royal Philharmonic recording as 1954. Applying those reissue data to this differently credited LP is an inference. No original session ledger or precise movement-by-movement day has been located. 1956 is the selected LP’s publication year, not an invented session date.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: Venue transcribed exactly from the reissue catalogue record. The original LP does not supply a venue. Its linkage to the selected LP is the same qualified inference as the session-date attribution; no more specific hall name is invented.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Not cleared as public domain in the EU or US; composition rights remain separate from the historic recording basis
fields.note: Shostakovich died in 1975. The ordinary EU life-plus-70 calculation runs through 2045; this is not a global clearance or a statement of a US expiry date. IMSLP identifies the work as non-public-domain in the EU and US. The inspected score is territorially hosted as public domain in Taiwan and is cited, not republished. No composition licence is asserted.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 3: territorial EU historic-recording basis; commercial circulation documented by December 1955, selected LP issue dated 1956
fields.note: The original Westminster sleeve/labels and album metadata establish the selected 1956 WN 18001/XWN 18001 issue. A visually inspected High Fidelity review, December 1955, p. 80, already names this London orchestra, Rodzinski, his second recording of the Fifth and Westminster catalogue 18001; the review prints SWN 18001 and erroneously calls the symphony D major, so those details are not silently normalized. The publisher also lists Nixa WLP 20004 in 1955. First lawful publication anywhere before 1963 is the rule; no EU-first-release claim is required or made. source.rights.published 1956 remains a conservative upper bound tied to the selected physical issue, not a first-release date. Even using 1956, the ordinary 50-year recording term had expired before the 2013 extension. US sound-recording status is not established. Complete item metadata, original side-transfer provenance and scans disclose no Creative Commons non-commercial condition or separate upstream digital source. This is not a worldwide public-domain or composition-rights clearance.

composer.epithet: Fifteen symphonies and fifteen quartets turn marches, fugues and a four-note signature into arguments about public ceremony and individual memory.
facts: Petrograd Conservatory from 1919: piano with Leonid Nikolayev, composition with Maximilian Steinberg
Leningrad Conservatory from 1937; Moscow Conservatory from 1943; dismissed from both in 1948
DSCH = D–E♭–C–B, using German note names
Fifteen symphonies · fifteen string quartets · six concertos · operas, songs and film scores
composer.background:
Dmitri Shostakovich was born in St Petersburg in 1906, the son of an engineer and a pianist. His mother, Sofiya, gave him his first piano lessons; in 1919 he entered the Petrograd Conservatory, where Leonid Nikolayev taught him piano and Maximilian Steinberg composition. The director, Alexander Glazunov, supported the young musician through the shortages following revolution and civil war. His father’s death in 1922 worsened the family’s finances, and Shostakovich earned money accompanying silent films. He graduated in piano in 1923 and composition in 1925: the graduation score was his First Symphony, written before his nineteenth birthday.

Nikolai Malko conducted its première in Leningrad on 12 May 1926. The orchestra includes a piano, whose abrupt interventions contribute to the symphonic argument. Clarinet, bassoon and trumpet exchange short phrases; a waltz can become a march without a change of personnel. International performances followed. Shostakovich still considered a performing career and received an honourable mention at the first Warsaw Chopin Competition in 1927. Thereafter his public piano appearances increasingly centred on his own works, including the concertos, chamber music and songs.
